html:
Uruk, in southern Iraq near the Euphrates, was the largest city in the world in the late 4th millennium BCE, perhaps home to some 40,000 people. Its age, about 4000 to 3100 BCE, is called the Uruk period.

Here appeared the things that make a civilisation: great temples on platforms, a ruling class, full-time craftsmen, cylinder seals and mass-produced pots. Around 3300 BCE scribes in Uruk's temples began to keep accounts on clay tablets, the first steps of cuneiform writing.

Uruk was one of the Sumerian city-states for thousands of years. Its legendary king, Gilgamesh, is the hero of the Epic of Gilgamesh, which praises its walls. It was finally abandoned in the early Islamic period. See also Iraq.
